title: Building Reusable Authorization Controls knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which security principle best applies to “Building Reusable Authorization Controls”?
options: Trust caller-controlled values and verify the control only on the successful happy path.
Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.
Rely on a hidden frontend control and skip backend verification because normal users cannot see the route.
Disable logs and tests so the security check cannot generate false positives.
questions.answer_key: Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.
questions.explanation: Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases. The other choices rely on obscurity, remove useful verification, or trust input that should be treated as untrusted.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing “Building Reusable Authorization Controls” in an application you own or an explicitly authorized local lab. Which approach gives the strongest evidence that the intended control works?
options: Write a focused test for the expected secure behavior and at least one relevant denied, malformed, expired, or failure case; record sanitized evidence.
Test only by looking at the page design and assume hidden controls are enforced.
Run broad tests against unrelated public systems to find a comparison point.
Record real credentials and tokens in the report to make reproduction easier.
questions.answer_key: Write a focused test for the expected secure behavior and at least one relevant denied, malformed, expired, or failure case; record sanitized evidence.
questions.explanation: A useful security check has a defined scope, expected behavior, negative/failure coverage, and sanitized evidence. Never expand testing beyond permission or store secrets in evidence.

questions.prompt: If a check related to “Building Reusable Authorization Controls” fails unexpectedly, what is the best next step?
options: Declare the entire application secure after a single successful request.
Change several unrelated settings at once and do not save the test conditions.
Suppress the finding without documenting why it is a false positive.
Reproduce with synthetic test data, compare expected and actual behavior, identify the root cause, apply a targeted fix, and retest neighboring paths.
questions.answer_key: Reproduce with synthetic test data, compare expected and actual behavior, identify the root cause, apply a targeted fix, and retest neighboring paths.
questions.explanation: Reducing the case and retaining reproducible sanitized evidence supports root-cause analysis. A targeted regression test helps prevent the issue from returning.
